accuracy.evidence: Brain model follows LeDoux's fast amygdala threat pathway with slower prefrontal appraisal; adrenaline acts within seconds while cortisol peaks roughly 20 to 30 minutes after a stressor (Dickerson and Kemeny 2004). Arnsten (2009) supports high catecholamine and cortisol levels impairing prefrontal working memory; adolescent reward sensitivity and prefrontal maturation into the mid-twenties follow Casey et al. (2008) and Steinberg (2008), labelled as average trends.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the myths pupils bring: that more stress always sharpens you (hormone slider shows recall collapsing at panic; quiz tag sharp), that blanking deletes memories (tag delete, practice p2 explanation), that teenage brains are broken (tag broken, m4), and that pretending everything is fine or not caring counts as reappraisal (reappraise step wrong cards, m10). The amygdala is framed as a detector that also flags good surprises, avoiding the 'fear centre' myth.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagbrain combines a dropped-surprise brain diagram where an alarm meter spikes before a delayed prefrontal check, an inverted-U hormone slider that removes recall bulbs, an age slider comparing reward and brake bars, a suppress or regulate sorter with an inside-stress gauge, and a thought-bubble reappraisal step. No other lab models brain regions or hormone dose; the shingle gate passed against every flag_*.js file.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes the learner cause the effect: they send surprises and watch the timing order, push hormones to panic and see facts fall out before finding the middling zone, visit ages 9, 15 and 25 to see the reward-brake gap open and close, and choose thoughts whose alarm level drops only when the new meaning is realistic. Feedback text names the mechanism every time.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting wrong answers: that the thinking prefrontal cortex reacts first, that more stress hormone always helps recall, that the prefrontal cortex is finished by about age 12, and that hiding a feeling switches it off. The step's own interaction disproves each one before the done message reveals the answer and reports the learner's guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with distractor tags (pfc, stem, delete, sharp, broken, amyg, hide, fake, same, health), each mapped to a specific corrective explanation pointing back to the lab step, for example that the brain stem runs breathing and heartbeat or that research links habitual suppression to lower wellbeing. A streak counter and Another button keep practice going.

readability.evidence: Learner audience targets met: the kid text uses short sentences, defines each term on first use (limbic system, amygdala, prefrontal cortex, dopamine, suppression, cognitive reappraisal) and uses concrete examples like the snake that is a stick. Adult text gives curriculum alignment, the key-terms list, the evidence base and the common mistakes in plain prose within the readability limit.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a distinct idea: brain parts and timing, stress and recall, adolescent development, and regulation strategies for the kid text; alignment, terms with evidence, mistakes, and the lab walk-through for the adult text. Practice and mastery items each test one mechanism, with numeric items modelling recall loss, cortisol timing, alarm reduction and years of prefrontal development.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at iPhone 13 and a 360 by 640 Android viewport in both themes show the brain labels wrapped inside the diagram, slider tracks with 13 pixel knobs inside large touch bands, two-line wrapped thought cards and event cards that fit the stage, and Show me runs finishing within the time limit. Every drag has a large button twin under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas aria-label mirrors every status line, button twins have descriptive labels such as 'Send to the brain: A loud bang behind you', and challenge feedback sits in a polite live region. Meter colours are paired with text labels (low, medium, high), reduced motion snaps tweens, and the axe checks pass in dark and light themes.
